title: From query acceleration to cache cooldown: Everything new in Fabric Data Warehouse
summary: A Build 2026 roundup post from the Fabric Data Warehouse team bundling a large wave of announcements: GPU-based query acceleration, configurable data-history retention, a rebuilt web/query-editing experience, several T-SQL language additions, transactional schema changes, faster SQL Analytics Endpoint sync, migration tooling updates, and a forward-looking list of near-term features including cache cooldown control and a lakehouse table health check.
audience: Data warehouse architects, platform owners, and DBAs deciding which upcoming Fabric Data Warehouse capabilities affect performance planning, retention/compliance policy, CI/CD process, or migration timelines.
why_it_matters: This single post is the most current, consolidated statement of the Fabric Data Warehouse roadmap direction as of the post date: it signals a shift toward GPU-accelerated query execution as a zero-code performance lever, gives warehouse owners new levers over cost/latency tradeoffs (retention windows, cache cooldown), and previews operational tooling (health checks, CI/CD scripting, statement routing) that changes how teams will manage warehouse capacity and schema lifecycle going forward.
takeaways: GPU-based query acceleration is coming to Fabric Data Warehouse as a no-code-change performance layer, with benchmarked gains reported against competing cloud warehouses.
Warehouse owners get new direct control over cost/latency tradeoffs through configurable data-history retention and (upcoming) cache cooldown duration.

A cluster of T-SQL surface-area additions (fuzzy string matching, concatenation operators, Unicode construction, procedural scalar UDFs, in-transaction ALTER TABLE) closes gaps with mainstream SQL Server/Synapse capabilities.
The SQL Analytics Endpoint gets a metadata-sync rework aimed at cutting data-freshness lag from minutes to seconds.
Several forthcoming items (cache cooldown, lakehouse table health check, statement-type routing, CI/CD scripting) are still in a 'coming soon' state at the time of this post and not yet shipped.

claims.text: Fabric announced GPU-based query acceleration for Data Warehouse as a coming-soon capability that requires no query rewrites, since the engine transparently offloads eligible SELECT operations such as large aggregations, joins, and scans to GPU hardware.

In benchmarks cited by the post, GPU-accelerated Fabric Data Warehouse was up to 7x faster than three unnamed leading cloud data warehouse competitors and held near-flat response times across a 22-query, 100 GB workload regardless of whether 1 or 64 users ran it concurrently.

Configurable Data History Retention, in preview at post time, lets administrators set a warehouse's retention window between 1 and 120 days via T-SQL, and that window governs time travel, point-in-time table clones, warehouse snapshots, and in-place restore.

Longer data-history retention windows trade higher storage cost for deeper recovery and historical query range, and shorter windows trade recovery depth for lower storage cost; this is described as an adjustable setting rather than a fixed platform limit.

The post announces a set of preview T-SQL additions: EDIT_DISTANCE-family string-matching functions, the || and ||= concatenation operators, the UNISTR Unicode-construction function, an ANY_VALUE aggregate, and a DATE_BUCKET date/time bucketing function.

Scalar user-defined functions in Fabric Data Warehouse gained preview support for procedural logic, including loops and multi-branch IF/THEN/ELSE, while remaining composable with CTEs, GROUP BY, HAVING, and ORDER BY in analytical queries.

ALTER TABLE operations inside explicit transactions reached general availability, allowing column add/drop, constraint changes, and multiple ALTER TABLE statements to be grouped into one atomic, all-or-nothing schema change.
A preview ALTER COLUMN capability allows widening numeric, time, string, and binary column types in place without a full table rewrite (CTAS), reducing the operational cost of routine schema changes.

Time Travel querying was extended, in preview, to the SQL Analytics Endpoint via a T-SQL OPTIONS clause, letting a single query read historical data as of a timestamp within the configured retention window.

The SQL Analytics Endpoint's metadata-sync architecture was rebuilt, in preview, to cut data-freshness lag from minutes to seconds for changes originating in Lakehouses and mirrored databases, enabled via a workspace setting.

As of this post, Cache Cooldown Configurability, a Lakehouse table health-check stored procedure, statement-type routing for Custom SQL Pools, and CI/CD scripting/Git integration for the SQL Analytics Endpoint were all listed as upcoming ('coming soon') rather than already shipped.

The planned Bulk Copy (BCP) API is described as enabling 5-10x higher client-side ingestion throughput than row-by-row INSERT statements by streaming data in batches and bypassing much of the standard per-statement query execution path.

Distributed Bitmap Filters, described for upcoming release, preemptively filter out non-matching fact-table rows before a join with a smaller dimension table; internal testing on two join-heavy, selective customer workloads reported 50-60% faster execution.
